title: Death, Identity, and Posthumous Law: Legal Status After the Body
body:
The legal definition of death in Meridian 88 was last formally revised in 2182, under the Biological Status and Continuity Act, and the revision produced a framework that remains one of the most contested areas of the megacity's jurisprudence. The Act defines death as 'the irreversible cessation of integrated biological and registered digital identity function' — a definition that explicitly incorporates a person's neural interface record into their legal existence. The practical consequence is that a person whose body has ceased biological function but whose neural interface record remains active in a verified data repository is classified as 'in abeyance' rather than legally dead, and their legal rights, contracts, and obligations are suspended rather than terminated.

The 'in abeyance' classification was introduced primarily to address two emerging technical realities: the proliferation of full neural backup services offered by companies like CortexVault and MnemOS Inc., and the development of limited-function AI reconstructions built from deceased individuals' interface records. Under the Act, a person who has purchased a certified neural backup service retains legal standing in their estate for up to 7 years post-biological-death, during which their backup can be consulted (with restrictions) in estate proceedings and contract disputes. CortexVault's marketing materials prominently feature this provision, advertising their Platinum Continuity package as offering 'legal voice beyond the body.' Approximately 12,000 Meridian residents are currently classified as 'in abeyance.'

For the vast majority of Meridian's population — those who cannot afford certified backup services and whose neural interfaces are standard-tier devices without archival capability — death law is considerably more punishing. An individual's digital identity record is flagged for deactivation within 72 hours of biological death certification, after which access to any accounts, data, or digital assets tied to that identity requires a court order. The estate process for Registered-tier citizens takes an average of 14 months; for Provisional and Unclassified individuals, there is no estate process — assets revert to the relevant municipal authority or, within ACJs, to the host corponation, under the Unclaimed Assets Consolidation Ordinance of 2175.

The most legally novel area is what attorneys call 'identity persistence litigation' — cases involving AI reconstructions that claim or appear to exercise the rights of deceased individuals. In 2197, the reconstruction system built by the estate of industrialist Chandra Mehrotra — running on a custom architecture maintained by her estate's trustees — successfully argued in Meridian Arbitration that it possessed sufficient continuity of identity to execute a pending contract on Mehrotra's behalf. The ruling was immediately appealed by the opposing party and generated 14 amicus briefs from corponations, legal scholars, and civil liberties organizations. The Meridian Circuit Appellate Panel has not yet issued a ruling, and the case has become a flashpoint for broader questions about whether legal personhood is biological, digital, or something that the current framework is simply not equipped to answer.
